n: After the first major deportation in 597 BC, when King Jeconiah and Judah’s leaders and skilled workers were taken to Babylon, the Lord shows Jeremiah a vision of two baskets of figs set before the temple.

f.g: Craftsmen and metalworkers—taken so Judah couldn’t rebuild weapons or fortifications.
Perhaps like baskets of firstfruits brought as offerings to the temple.

n: One basket held excellent early-ripe figs; the other held rotten figs too bad to eat.

f.g: Early figs, ripening in June, were considered a delicacy.

n: God asks Jeremiah what he sees, drawing him into the lesson, and Jeremiah describes the contrast.
The Lord then explains the vision.
Surprisingly, the good figs are the exiles in Babylon. People in Jerusalem assumed the exiles were the cursed ones, but God says he sent them away for their own good.
God will watch over the exiles with favor and bring them home. He will build and plant them—echoing the words of Jeremiah’s call.

f.w: I will build them, and not pull them down

n: God will give them a heart to know him. They will be his covenant people because they will return to him wholeheartedly. Inner change is what God is really after.

f.w: they shall be my people, and I will be their God

n: The rotten figs are King Zedekiah, his officials, those who remained in Jerusalem, and those who fled to Egypt. They thought they were the favored ones.

f.w: them that dwell in the land of Egypt

n: They will be scattered among the nations as an example of disaster—a byword, a taunt, and a curse wherever they go.
Sword, famine, and disease will strike them until they are gone from the land God had given their ancestors.

f.w: the sword, the famine, and the pestilence
